prerequisites: Prior knowledge and learning outcomes related to fluid movement (liquids and gases) and energy transfer processes, including basic operation principles of incompressible fluid machines.

Recommended prior courses: Engineering degrees in Industrial, Mining, or Civil branches, and the compulsory course 'Aprovechamiento Energético de Recursos Hidráulicos y Eólicos' from the first semester of the Master's Degree in Energy Engineering.

learning_outcomes.text: Possess and understand knowledge that provides a basis or opportunity to be original in the development and/or application of ideas, often in a research context.
Students should know how to apply acquired knowledge and problem-solving skills in new or unfamiliar environments within broader (or multidisciplinary) contexts related to their field of study.

Students should be able to integrate knowledge and confront the complexity of formulating judgments based on incomplete or limited information, including reflections on the social and ethical responsibilities linked to the application of their knowledge and judgments.
Students should know how to communicate their conclusions and the ultimate knowledge and reasons that support them to specialized and non-specialized audiences clearly and unambiguously.
Students should possess learning skills that allow them to continue studying in a largely self-directed or autonomous manner.
Problem-solving in new or unfamiliar environments within multidisciplinary contexts related to energy engineering.
Ability to integrate knowledge to formulate applications for the development of new energy technologies.
Autonomous learning ability that allows continued study through the search and assimilation of specialized documentation in scientific-technical literature.
Performance of elementary calculations for sizing, selection of machines and equipment, and operation for fluid installations with energy transfers.
Ability to study, propose, and apply different types of technologies to improve the utilization and energy efficiency of installations or plants, comparing alternatives by performance and costs.

Analyze, design, and project fluid installations in the fields of industry, building, public works, energy generation, and transport, selecting solutions that maximize energy efficiency among available technological alternatives.
Know and apply legislation, regulations, and technical codes related to fluid installation projects.
Evaluate and minimize the environmental and social impacts of actions and projects related to fluid installations, paying special attention to energy efficiency criteria.

syllabus_topics: Energy transfers and efficiency in installations with fluid machines.
Regulation, similarity, and cavitation in pumping systems.
Air quality and energy efficiency in ventilation systems.
Energy efficiency in industrial ventilation systems, pneumatic transport, and particle separation.
Energy efficiency, particular cases: closed circuits, hydraulic drives, compressed air installations, and consumption measurement.
Operation of a pump on a test bench (obtaining characteristic curves, checking similarity laws, consumption dependence)
Case study: operation of a pumping installation for minimum consumption, with and without suction conditions.
Case study: design of a suction system, pneumatic transport, and particle separation with minimum consumption.
Case study: numerical analysis of ventilation (natural and forced) of a warehouse with a thermal source.

assessment_methods.method: Practical work (T1): individual work on hydraulic systems (themes 1 and 2), related to minimum consumption operation of a pumping system with parallel and variable speed pumps, with individual specifications. Structured in three deliverables.

Practical work (T2): individual work on ventilation and pneumatic particle transport (themes 3 and 4), related to design and sizing for minimum consumption of pneumatic transport systems with variable speed centrifugal fan and cyclone particle separation, with individual specifications. Structured in three deliverables.

Practical work (T3): group work (up to three students) associated with the first laboratory practice, on testing a centrifugal pump for characteristic curve determination, consumption analysis, and similarity law verification. One final deliverable per group.

Practical work (T4): pair work associated with the laboratory practice on numerical analysis of ventilation (natural and forced) of an industrial warehouse with a thermal source, with a final presentation.
Optional final exam, with questions and numerical exercises on all course content.

assessment_rules: The final grade (NF) in the ordinary call is calculated as: NF = 0.3 * (T1 + T2 + T4) + 0.1 * T3, where each practical work grade is out of 10 points. If NF reaches at least 5 points, the course is passed, and the final exam is not required. If NF is below 5 points, the final exam must be taken, which will count for 10 points. For the extraordinary call, the final grade will be solely from a written final exam (maximum 10 points). Students with differentiated assessment (who did not complete the continuous assessment activities) must take the final exam.
